Training Module 11 - Firmware Project

Hi everyone! Welcome to Firmware, this will be the official Firmware Onboarding Project. Make sure you have read through at least all of the firmware modules before completing this.

Outcomes:

After this module members should be able to 

  1. Set up a new PlatformIO project
  2. Understand the bare basic of C++ code
  3. Understand how data moves through the code
  4. be able to send and receive SPI frames
  5. be able to read analog values

Getting Started

  1. Please read this page on PlatformIO: LINK
  2. To install Virtual Studio Code (VSCode), which is the recommend text editor please read this: LINK
  3. For those who are completely new to code, please read this link to install git on your computer: LINK
Step 1: Fork the repo

Click this LINK to our team GitHub repository. This is where your submission will live. You should see something like the image below.

Click Fork in the top right corner. Once it finishes, you'll land on your own copy of the repo, which should look something like this:

Step 2: Clone your fork

Now we'll download your fork onto your computer so you can actually work on it.

  1. On your forked repo's page, click the green Code button and copy the HTTPS URL.
  2. Open your terminal (Terminal on Mac, PowerShell or Git Bash on Windows).
  3. Run:
git clone <the URL you just copied>

For example (don't copy this one directly, use the URL from your own fork):

git clone https://github.com/your-username/firmware-onboarding.git

This creates a folder on your machine with a full copy of the repo, ready to work in.

Creating a PlatformIO Project

Open VSCode and navigate yourself to the "PIO Home" page. From there, please create a new project.

This will open up the Project Wizard.

  1. Name: use the format LAST_FIRST_Firmware_Onboarding (e.g. Liu_Anthony_Firmware_Onboarding).
  2. Board: select Arduino Uno.
  3. Framework: should auto-select Arduino, just double check it did.
  4. Location: uncheck "Use default location" and browse to the submissions/ folder inside the repo you just cloned, then create a folder there named like this: submissions/LAST_FIRST/. This is what makes sure your project ends up inside the repo instead of somewhere PlatformIO defaults to on its own.
  5. Click Finish.

At this point you've created your first PlatformIO project, congrats! You generally won't need to create PlatformIO projects from scratch on this team, but it's good to know how.

Familiarize Yourself With The IDE

For those new, this explains the IDE:

  1. This is where all your installed extensions live (the ant icon is PlatformIO). Recommended extensions to install:
    • GitHub Pull Requests — Create and review pull requests without leaving VS Code
    • GitLens — Does a lot, but the main thing you'll use it for is seeing who wrote each line of code and when
  2. File Explorer (left sidebar) — shows the files in your project
  3. Editor (main pane) — where your currently open file is displayed and edited
  4. Panel (bottom) — your command area
    • Terminal tab: where you'll run most commands
    • Problems tab: useful for spotting what's going wrong in your code
  5. Tabs (top of editor) — open files appear here, so VS Code behaves a bit like a browser with multiple tabs
  6. Status bar (bottom) — shows Git info and PlatformIO commands in one convenient place

Project Overview:

In this project, you'll develop code that 1) reads live temperature data from a BME280 sensor and 2) drive an LED's blink rate. The idea is that the LED blinks faster as it gets warmer, slower as it cools. You'll read the sensor twice: over I2C and then SPI, so you get hands-on experience with two common protocols. 

Setup The .ini File

For the platformio.ini file, go ahead and just copy this block of code:

[env]
platform = atmelavr
board = uno
framework = arduino
monitor_speed = 115200
build_flags =
    -D ETL_NO_STL
    -Iinclude
lib_deps =
    etlcpp/Embedded Template Library@20.39.4
    adafruit/Adafruit BME280 Library@^2.2.4
    adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor@^1.1.14
    adafruit/Adafruit BusIO@^1.15.0

[env:uno_i2c]
build_src_filter = +<*> -<main_spi.cpp>

[env:uno_spi]
build_src_filter = +<*> -<main_i2c.cpp>

What's being done here is just setting up the environment. The most important part is the lib_deps section. Here, we're declaring that this project needs the Adafruit BME280, Unified Sensor, and BusIO libraries. Something you'll learn over time is that a lot of what you need already exists as pre-built libraries — they handle the lower-level requirements for you, so all you really need to do is use the functions they provide.

Setup The File Structure

For our team, we will always make the distinction between interfaces and systems. 

Notice here we have separate files for systems and interfaces.

  • Interfaces are meant to be how we communicate with the hardware. They should not have any logic and they should not be making decisions. Their only job is to communicate with hardware and collect data.
  • Systems are where all the real logic belongs. The systems take the data the interfaces collect and determine what should happen.

So here, we have BMEI2CInterface and BMESPIInterface — these interfaces let us communicate with the BME280 sensor using I2C or SPI. They store whatever data they collect, which is then used by the LEDController system. This LED controller is what determines the rate of the LED's blinks. This separation between interfaces and systems matters because, by keeping the hardware-facing code separate, we can test the logic without needing any hardware at all — just on your computer.

BMEConstants.h

In this file, we store the global constants for the project. In general, the include/ folder is where we put project-wide data that many different files need access to — constants, task/config structs, that sort of thing.

A few things worth understanding about why this file exists and lives where it does: We want to pull constants into different files because there are multiple files that need these variables. If certain constants were hardcoded into the file each time, every time we wanted to change it, we would need to do it in multiple places. With one shared file, you change the value once, and everything that depends on it stays correct automatically. We use the include/ folder because it is meant to be the one folder every part of the project can reasonably need to reach — both your main.cpp files in src/, and your interface/system code under lib/. 

Your file might look something like this:

#pragma once
#include <Arduino.h>

namespace BMEConstants
{
    // constants here!
}
Interface Files

Now let's get started with code! In C++, code is split across two kinds of files:

  • Header files (.h) — You can think of these as a table of contents. They declare what exists (function names, their inputs and outputs, class definitions) without actually writing out how any of it works.
  • Source files (.cpp) — This is where the actual logic lives. Every function declared in a .h file gets its real implementation written out here.

For example, BMEI2CInterface.h declares what our I2C interface can do, without saying how. The how is defined by the cpp file. Below is an example of a general header file.

At the top, #pragma once is how we ensure only one copy of this file gets processed by the compiler, even if it's included from multiple places. The #include line is how the compiler brings in declarations from another file. In essence, it literally pulls in/copies the BMEConstants, Adafruit_BME280, and singleton files into this one.

For those completely new to C++ and code: C++ is a compiled language. In general, there are two broad types of languages: compiled and interpreted.

  • In a compiled language, a compiler reads your entire program ahead of time and translates it into machine code the processor can run directly. Think of it as connecting all the dots first, then handing off a finished, ready-to-run program.
  • In an interpreted language, there's no separate translation step. An interpreter reads and executes your code line by line, on the spot, as the program runs.
#pragma once
#include <Adafruit_BME280.h>
#include <etl/singleton.h>
#include "BMEConstants.h"


class BMEI2CInterface
{
public:

    BMEI2CInterface() = default;

    // Code here!

private:

   // Code here!

};
using BMEI2CInterfaceInstance = etl::singleton<BMEI2CInterface>;

From here, we're going to let you try the project yourself! My biggest tip: look at the Adafruit_BME280.h library. To do that, Cmd/Ctrl-click on it — it should open up the entire library, which defines essentially everything you need to work with.

A few things worth specifically looking for once you're in there:

  • The constructors. There are three of them. Reading these tells you exactly what arguments each mode needs, before you write a single line of your own code.
  • begin(). This is what actually talks to the sensor and confirms it's there. Notice what it returns — that return type tells you how to detect a wiring failure.

You don't need to understand every line of this library since most of it (calibration coefficients, register addresses) is implementation details Adafruit already solved for you. What you're looking for is the public interface: which functions are you actually allowed to call, and what do they need from you.

In the end, you should have two complete interfaces (header and source) — one for I2C and one for SPI. Good luck, and let any of the leads know if you have questions.

Checking Your Code Builds

Remember above how I said C++ is a compiled language? What we can do is build/compile our code to make sure it meets the compiler's requirements. This catches mistakes before you ever try to flash anything to real hardware.

To build our code, the first thing we want to do is check our environment. In the bottom bar, select either environment. Then click the checkmark icon to the left of it; this will build your environment and download any necessary dependencies.

Note this is the UI version of doing it. It's good to know that, in the background, what clicking that checkmark actually does is run:

pio run -e <environment_name>

pio run is the underlying command that does the building. The -e flag is how you specify which environment to build. Makes sense, right?

What's actually happening when you build: the compiler is translating every .cpp file into machine code the chip on the uno can actually execute, then linking all of those pieces together into one program. Along the way, it check that every function you called actually exists, every type matches what it's supposed to be, and every file you tried to #include was actually found. A successful build doesn't mean your logic is correct, but just that the code is structurally valid C++. Whether it actually behaves the way you intended only gets confirmed once you flash it to real hardware and watch what happens.

If your code doesn't build, it should tell you exactly what's wrong. For example, here it shows the build failed, and displays exactly what went wrong. If you Cmd/Ctrl-click the error, it'll take you straight to the exact line causing the issue!

One habit worth building early: build often, not just at the end. Write a small piece, build, confirm it compiles, then move to the next piece. 

Systems Files

Conceptually, this file looks the same as the interface files. The only difference, again, is that systems are all about business logic. So, how does the LED's blink rate change based on temperature? That question is entirely what LEDController is responsible for answering.

Notice what LEDController does not know anything about: it doesn't know if the temperature came from I2C or SPI, it doesn't know what a BME280 even is. It just takes a number (a temperature reading) and decides what to do with it (how fast to blink). That's the whole point of the interfaces/systems split, LEDController doesn't care how we got the temperature, only what the temperature currently is.

Again, please constantly build your code!

Main Files

The main file is essentially what determines what code actually runs. The general structure of main is this:

#include <Arduino.h>
#include "BMEI2CInterface.h"
#include "LEDController.h"
#include "BMEConstants.h"


void setup()
{
    // Code here!
}

void loop()
{
    // Code here!
}

The names of the sections are pretty self-explanatory. The setup() section is where you set up the necessary parameters or objects. It runs only once, right when the board powers on or resets. The loop() section is, well, a loop — it will continuously run that code again and again, for as long as the board has power.

Testing/Submitting

At this point, you might be ready to test/submit your code! To do that, you are going to need to push your code and then reate the PR

Step 1 — Commit Your Changes

Open the terminal (same one you've been using for pio run) and run these from inside your cloned repo:

git add .
git commit -m "Add BME280 I2C and SPI interfaces with LED blink rate"

git add . stages every changed file — it tells git "these are the changes I want to save." git commit actually saves that snapshot, with a short message describing what you did. Generally, we always want to write a message that would actually mean something to a reviewer glancing at your commit history later, not just "done" or "fix."

Step 2 — Push Your Branch To Your Fork
git push

Remember from earlier: your local clone points at your fork, not the original team repo. So this uploads your commit to your own GitHub copy, where it's safe and backed up, but not yet visible to anyone reviewing the original repo.

Step 3 — Open The Pull Request

Go to your fork on GitHub. Click on Contriubte, then you can create a new Pull request. 

From here it will open up this: 

Note, here this opens the PR template automatically — please fill it out completely. For the title please go with this format: LAST_FIRST_Submission

Step 4 — What Happens Next

Once your PR is open, two things happen automatically:

  1. CI runs your build. GitHub Actions will try to build your submission the same way pio run does locally — if it fails here even though it worked on your machine, don't panic, it usually means something environment-specific (a file that got .gitignore'd that shouldn't have been, for example). Click into the failed check for the exact error, same as reading a local build failure.
  2. A reviewer gets requested automatically. But beyond that, please just let a lead know your code is ready to be tested.

This is what it should look like: 

If you've test your code, and if everything works, we'll approve and merge the PR — that's essentially the confirmation that you've completed the project!

CONGRATS YOUR DONE!


For Reviewers!

Completion = approval, not merge. To avoid every trainee's finished solution becoming permanently browsable to everyone else in main, we don't actually merge submission PRs. Once you've reviewed and are satisfied, approve the PR, then close it without merging. The code will stay on the trainee's own fork.

Always add the completed label before closing. A closed PR shows the same plain "Closed" state in the PR list whether it was approved or just abandoned, so there's no visual difference at a glance. Approving first does leave a permanent record (visible once you open the PR itself), but it's easy to miss when scanning the list. Adding a completed label right before closing makes finished submissions instantly scannable from the PR list view, instead of requiring anyone to open each closed PR individually to check. You can add it on the right side, like this:
